                "__tool_use_purpose": "Build/vet/fmt and verify the delete flow: confirm deletes + persists, cancel is a no-op, session terminated.",
                "command": "go build ./... && go vet ./... && test -z \"$(gofmt -l .)\" && echo \"---BUILD/VET/FMT OK---\"\ncat > ui/zz_del_test.go <<'EOF'\npackage ui\n\nimport (\n\t\"os\"\n\t\"path/filepath\"\n\t\"testing\"\n\n\t\"github.com/hampusgrimskar/taco/repos\"\n)\n\nfunc seed(t *testing.T) {\n\ttmp := t.TempDir()\n\tos.Setenv(\"HOME\", tmp)\n\tif err := repos.Init(); err != nil { t.Fatal(err) }\n\trepos.Instance = []*repos.Repo{\n\t\t{Alias: \"api\", Path: \"/src/api\"},\n\t\t{Alias: \"web\", Path: \"/src/web\"},\n\t}\n\t// persist so filePath is set for sync\n\t_ = filepath.Join\n}\n\nfunc TestDeleteConfirmRemoves(t *testing.T) {\n\tseed(t)\n\tvar m model\n\tm.activeTab = TabRepos\n\t// cursor on first ordered repo (api)\n\tm.openDeleteDialog()\n\tif !m.deleting || m.del.alias == \"\" {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"dialog did not open\")\n\t}\n\ttarget := m.del.alias\n\t// focus Delete and confirm\n\tm.updateDeleteDialog(\"right\") // move focus (Cancel->Delete or Delete->Cancel)\n\t// ensure focus is on Delete (buttonSave)\n\tif m.del.confirm != buttonSave {\n\t\tm.updateDeleteDialog(\"left\")\n\t}\n\t// use explicit 'y' to be deterministic\n\tm.updateDeleteDialog(\"y\")\n\tif m.deleting {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"dialog should close after delete\")\n\t}\n\tif repos.Find(target) != nil {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"repo %q should be deleted\", target)\n\t}\n\tif len(repos.All()) != 1 {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"expected 1 repo left, got %d\", len(repos.All()))\n\t}\n}\n\nfunc TestDeleteCancelKeepsRepo(t *testing.T) {\n\tseed(t)\n\tvar m model\n\tm.activeTab = TabRepos\n\tm.openDeleteDialog()\n\ttarget := m.del.alias\n\tm.updateDeleteDialog(\"n\") // cancel\n\tif m.deleting {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"dialog should close on cancel\")\n\t}\n\tif repos.Find(target) == nil {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"repo %q should still exist after cancel\", target)\n\t}\n\tif len(repos.All()) != 2 {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"expected 2 repos, got %d\", len(repos.All()))\n\t}\n}\n\nfunc TestDeleteDefaultFocusIsCancel(t *testing.T) {\n\tseed(t)\n\tvar m model\n\tm.activeTab = TabRepos\n\tm.openDeleteDialog()\n\tif m.del.confirm != buttonCancel {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"default focus should be Cancel (safe), got %v\", m.del.confirm)\n\t}\n}\nEOF\ngo test ./ui/ -run 'TestDelete' -v 2>&1 | tail -15\nrm -f ui/zz_del_test.go",
                "working_dir": "/Users/egriham/repos/misc/taco"
              }
            }

            "data": "Verified (tests removed):\n- **Confirm deletes + persists** — confirming removes the repo, closes the dialog, and leaves the correct remaining repos. ✓\n- **Cancel is a no-op** — `n`/Esc closes the dialog and keeps the repo. ✓\n- **Default focus is Cancel** — the safe choice is pre-selected so an accidental Enter doesn't delete. ✓\n\nFeature summary — `Ctrl+D` on a selected repo:\n- Opens a red-bordered confirmation modal: *\"Delete repo — Remove «alias» from taco?\"* with **Cancel** / **Delete** buttons.\n- Modal: `←`/`→`/`Tab` switch buttons, `Enter` activates the focused one, `y` deletes, `n`/`Esc` cancels. Default focus is **Cancel**.\n- On confirm: if the repo has a live tmux session, it's **terminated first** (so we don't orphan it), then the repo is removed and persisted, and the cursor is clamped to stay valid.\n\nBuilds, vets, gofmt-clean.\n\n**Verification status:** the delete logic (confirm/cancel/persist/focus) is test-verified. The session-termination-on-delete path runs a real `tmux kill-session` and the modal rendering both need a live TTY — please run `go run .`, add a repo, start its session with Enter, come back, and `Ctrl+D` it to confirm the session is killed and the entry is removed. The confirmation dialog visuals should also be checked there."

              "content": [
                {
                  "kind": "text",
                  "data": "\n\t// Find the longest alias so the indicator column aligns, then place the\n\t// indicator 5 positions to the right of it.\n\tlongest := 0\n\tfor _, repo := range ordered {\n\t\tif len(repo.Alias) > longest {\n\t\t\tlongest = len(repo.Alias)\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\tindicatorCol := longest + 5\n\n\ttotal := len(ordered)\n\trows := visibleItemRows(total, visibleRows)\n\n\t// Window using the persistent scroll offset; clamp defensively in case the\n\t// terminal was resized since the last cursor move.\n\tstart := m.repoScroll\n\tif start > total-rows {\n\t\tstart = total - rows\n\t}\n\tif start < 0 {\n\t\tstart = 0\n\t}\n\tend := start + rows\n\tif end > total {\n\t\tend = total\n\t}\n\n\t// Build exactly visibleRows lines so the panel height never changes as\n\t// scroll hints appear or disappear. When scrolling is possible, the first\n\t// and last lines are reserved as hint slots (blank when not scrolled).\n\tlines := make([]string, 0, visibleRows)\n\n\tscrollable := total > visibleRows\n\tif scrollable {\n\t\tif start > 0 {\n\t\t\tlines = append(lines, muted(\"  ↑ more\"))\n\t\t} else {\n\t\t\tlines = append(lines, \"\")\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\tfor i := start; i < end; i++ {\n\t\trepo := ordered[i]\n\t\tlines = append(lines, RepoRow(repo.Alias, indicatorCol, repo.Session != nil, m.repoCursor == i))\n\t}\n\n\tif scrollable {\n\t\tif end < total {\n\t\t\tlines = append(lines, muted(\"  ↓ more\"))\n\t\t} else {\n\t\t\tlines = append(lines, \"\")\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\t// Pad with blank lines so the body is always exactly visibleRows tall.\n\tfor len(lines) < visibleRows {\n\t\tlines = append(lines, \"\")\n\t}\n"
                }
              ],
              "status": "success"
            }

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "I see the design tension clearly now. The full-height padding was added specifically to keep the box height stable when scroll hints toggle. If I remove it and rely on `PanelCentered` + `Panel`'s fixed `.Height()`, the box height stays fixed anyway (because `.Height()` sets it), and the compact centered block will genuinely appear centered.\n\nBut there's a catch: when the list **is** scrollable and fills the height, padding vs no-padding is the same. When the list is **short** (fewer repos than height), removing padding lets `PanelCentered` center the short block — which is exactly what you want. When scrollable, the block equals the height, so centering is a no-op — also fine.\n\nSo the fix: remove the full-height padding. `Panel`'s `.Height(panelHeight)` inside `PanelCentered` still fixes the outer box height, so it won't shrink. Let me remove the padding loop:"

            "data": {

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "Performance is not a concern at all — this is a terminal UI redrawing a few dozen lines of text on keypress. There's no rendering cost worth worrying about; a side info panel adds a handful of string operations per frame. So go for it purely on UX grounds.\n\nLet me think about the layout and what to show, then confirm with you before building.\n\n**Layout:** split the panel area horizontally into two boxes side by side using `lipgloss.JoinHorizontal`:\n- **Left** — the repo list (narrower now, e.g. ~40% or a fixed width).\n- **Right** — an info panel for the highlighted repo.\n\nThe width math needs care: the two boxes plus their borders must sum to `m.width`. I'd give the list a share and the info panel the rest, both using the same `panelInner`-style border/padding accounting we already have. The search box and footer stay full-width below.\n\n**What to show in the info panel** — this is the real question. Options, given what a `Repo` currently holds (`Alias`, `Path`, `Session`):\n- **Alias** and full **path** (path is often truncated in the list, so showing it in full here is genuinely useful)\n- **Session status** — active/inactive, and the session ID if running\n- Cheap **git info** read live from the repo: current branch, dirty/clean, last commit. This is the most valuable content, but it means running `git` (or reading `.git/HEAD`) per highlighted repo. Reading `.git/HEAD` for the branch is basically free; running `git status` is heavier but still fine if done lazily (only for the highlighted repo, maybe cached).\n\n**A design decision to make:** how much git info, and how to fetch it.\n- **Minimal (zero cost):** alias, full path, session status, branch (read from `.git/HEAD` directly — a single small file read, no subprocess).\n- **Richer (small cost):** add dirty/clean and last-commit via `git`, run as an async `tea.Cmd` when the highlight changes so it never blocks the UI, with a cache keyed by path.\n\nMy recommendation: start with the **minimal, zero-subprocess** version (alias, path, session, branch from `.git/HEAD`). It's instant, needs no async machinery, and already makes the space useful. We can layer in async `git status` later if you want dirty-state/commit info.\n\nTwo things I want your call on before I build:\n1. **What content** — minimal (alias/path/session/branch) to start, or do you want the richer git status/last-commit now (async)?\n2. **Behavior on narrow terminals** — if the terminal is too narrow to fit both boxes reasonably, should I collapse back to the single full-width list? (I'd recommend yes, with a width threshold.)\n\nOnce you confirm those, I'll implement it."
          }
        ]
      }

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "Good — git info it is: current branch and the last 5 commit titles. Let me think about how to fetch it, because that decision shapes the implementation.\n\n**Branch** — cheap: read `.git/HEAD`, which contains `ref: refs/heads/<branch>`. A single small file read, no subprocess. (Detached HEAD would contain a raw SHA; I'll handle that.)\n\n**Last 5 commit titles** — this needs `git log --format=%s -n 5`. That's a subprocess. Two ways to run it:\n- **Async** (`tea.Cmd`): fire it when the highlight changes, deliver results via a message, cache by path. Never blocks the UI even on a slow/large repo. More machinery.\n- **Synchronous**: run it inline in `View`/on cursor move. Simpler, but `git log` runs on every highlight change and *could* stutter on a huge repo or slow disk, and running it in `View` (which fires every frame) would be wasteful.\n\nThe right approach is **async with a cache**: when the highlighted repo changes, kick off a `tea.Cmd` that runs `git log` for that path; store the result keyed by path so re-highlighting is instant and we don't re-run. This keeps the UI responsive regardless of repo size.\n\n**Layout:** split the panel row into list (left) + info (right) via `JoinHorizontal`, with a width threshold to collapse to just the list on narrow terminals (you didn't object, and it avoids a cramped mess).\n\nHere's my plan:\n\n1. **`repos` package**: `GitBranch(path) string` (reads `.git/HEAD`) and `GitRecentCommits(path, n) []string` (runs `git log`). Both tolerate non-repos / errors gracefully.\n2. **`ui`**: an async `tea.Cmd` (`gitInfoCmd`) + a `gitInfoMsg{path, branch, commits, err}`, a cache `map[string]gitInfo` on the model, and logic to trigger the fetch when the highlighted repo's path changes.\n3. **Rendering**: an info panel (`renderRepoInfo`) showing branch + commit titles; `View` joins list + info horizontally, collapsing on narrow width.\n4. **Triggering**: on `moveCursor` and after launch/return, if the highlighted repo's info isn't cached, emit the fetch `Cmd`.\n\nOne implementation nuance: `moveCursor` currently returns nothing (it's called from the key switch which returns `m, nil`). To fire an async `Cmd` on highlight change, I'll have the relevant key cases return the `Cmd`. I'll compute \"did the highlighted repo change, and is its info uncached?\" and return `gitInfoCmd` when so.\n\nBefore I build — one quick confirmation: **collapse the info panel on narrow terminals** (below some width, show just the list), yes? And is a threshold around 80 columns reasonable, or do you want it always shown? Once you confirm I'll implement the whole thing."
          }
        ]
      }

                "content": "\n// GitBranch returns the current branch name of the repo at path by reading\n// .git/HEAD directly (no subprocess). For a detached HEAD it returns a short\n// commit SHA. Returns \"\" if it cannot be determined.\nfunc GitBranch(path string) string {\n\tdata, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(path, \".git\", \"HEAD\"))\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\treturn \"\"\n\t}\n\thead := strings.TrimSpace(string(data))\n\tif ref, ok := strings.CutPrefix(head, \"ref: refs/heads/\"); ok {\n\t\treturn ref\n\t}\n\t// Detached HEAD: head is a raw SHA.\n\tif len(head) >= 7 {\n\t\treturn head[:7]\n\t}\n\treturn head\n}\n\n// GitRecentCommits returns up to n recent commit subject lines for the repo at\n// path, newest first. Returns nil (no error) if git is unavailable or the\n// command fails, so callers can render gracefully.\nfunc GitRecentCommits(path string, n int) []string {\n\tcmd := exec.Command(\"git\", \"-C\", path, \"log\", fmt.Sprintf(\"-n%d\", n), \"--format=%s\")\n\tout, err := cmd.Output()\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\treturn nil\n\t}\n\tlines := strings.Split(strings.TrimRight(string(out), \"\\n\"), \"\\n\")\n\tif len(lines) == 1 && lines[0] == \"\" {\n\t\treturn nil\n\t}\n\treturn lines\n}\n"

Narrower than this, the list takes the full width.\nconst infoWidthThreshold = 90\n\n// infoPanelWidth is the outer width of the info panel.\nconst infoPanelWidth = 40\n\n// --- extensible section model ---\n//\n// The info panel is composed of independent sections. To add or remove\n// information, add or remove an entry in infoSections — each section decides\n// its own title and how to render its body from the given repo + git info.\n\n// infoSection is one titled block in the info panel.\ntype infoSection struct {\n\ttitle  string\n\trender func(repo *repos.Repo, info gitInfo) string\n}\n\n// infoSections is the ordered list of sections shown in the info panel.\n// Append or remove entries here to change what the panel displays.\nvar infoSections = []infoSection{\n\t{\n\t\ttitle: \"Branch\",\n\t\trender: func(_ *repos.Repo, info gitInfo) string {\n\t\t\tif info.branch == \"\" {\n\t\t\t\treturn muted(\"—\")\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\treturn infoBranchStyle.Render(info.branch)\n\t\t},\n\t},\n\t{\n\t\ttitle: \"Recent commits\",\n\t\trender: func(_ *repos.Repo, info gitInfo) string {\n\t\t\tif len(info.commits) == 0 {\n\t\t\t\treturn muted(\"—\")\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tlines := make([]string, len(info.commits))\n\t\t\tfor i, c := range info.commits {\n\t\t\t\tlines[i] = \"• \" + c\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\treturn lipgloss.JoinVertical(lipgloss.Left, lines...)\n\t\t},\n\t},\n}\n\n// --- styles ---\n\nvar (\n\tinfoPanelStyle = lipgloss.NewStyle().\n\t\t\tBorder(lipgloss.RoundedBorder()).\n\t\t\tBorderForeground(colorBorder).\n\t\t\tPadding(1, 2)\n\n\tinfoSectionTitleStyle = lipgloss.NewStyle().Bold(true).Foreground(colorAccent)\n\n\tinfoBranchStyle = lipgloss.NewStyle().Foreground(lipgloss.Color(\"42\")) // green\n)\n\n// renderRepoInfo renders the info panel for the given repo, sized to the panel\n// height.                 {
                  "kind": "text",
                  "data": "}\n\nfunc (m model) Update(msg tea.Msg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {\n\tswitch msg := msg.(type) {\n\tcase tea.WindowSizeMsg:\n\t\tm.width = msg.Width\n\t\tm.height = msg.Height\n\n\tcase sessionFinishedMsg:\n\t\t// tmux exited (user detached or session ended); bubbletea resumed.\n\t\t// The launched repo has moved to the top, so follow it with the cursor.\n\t\tm.lastErr = msg.err\n\t\tif m.launchedAlias != \"\" {\n\t\t\tordered := orderedRepos(m.query)\n\t\t\tfor i, repo := range ordered {\n\t\t\t\tif repo.Alias == m.launchedAlias {\n\t\t\t\t\tm.repoCursor = i\n\t\t\t\t\tbreak\n\t\t\t\t}\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t\tm.clampScroll(len(ordered))\n\t\t\tm.launchedAlias = \"\"\n\t\t}\n\n\tcase scanDoneMsg:\n\t\tm.onScanDone(msg)\n\n\tcase tea.KeyPressMsg:\n\t\tkey := msg.String()\n"
                }
              ],
              "status": "success"
            }
          }
        ],

              "input": {
                "__tool_use_purpose": "Test git helpers against a real temp git repo, and the info-panel caching/section rendering + collapse behavior.",
                "command": "cat > repos/zz_git_test.go <<'EOF'\npackage repos\n\nimport (\n\t\"os/exec\"\n\t\"testing\"\n)\n\nfunc TestGitBranchAndCommits(t *testing.T) {\n\tdir := t.TempDir()\n\trun := func(args ...string) {\n\t\tc := exec.Command(\"git\", append([]string{\"-C\", dir}, args...)...)\n\t\tc.Env = append(c.Environ(),\n\t\t\t\"GIT_AUTHOR_NAME=t\", \"GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL=t@t\",\n\t\t\t\"GIT_COMMITTER_NAME=t\", \"GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL=t@t\")\n\t\tif out, err := c.CombinedOutput(); err != nil {\n\t\t\tt.Fatalf(\"git %v: %v\\n%s\", args, err, out)\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\trun(\"init\", \"-b\", \"main\")\n\trun(\"commit\", \"--allow-empty\", \"-m\", \"first commit\")\n\trun(\"commit\", \"--allow-empty\", \"-m\", \"second commit\")\n\n\tif b := GitBranch(dir); b != \"main\" {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"branch = %q, want main\", b)\n\t}\n\tcommits := GitRecentCommits(dir, 5)\n\tif len(commits) != 2 || commits[0] != \"second commit\" || commits[1] != \"first commit\" {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"commits = %v\", commits)\n\t}\n\t// Non-repo path returns empty gracefully.\n\tif GitBranch(t.TempDir()) != \"\" || GitRecentCommits(t.TempDir(), 5) != nil {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"non-repo should return empty\")\n\t}\n}\nEOF\ngo test ./repos/ -run TestGitBranchAndCommits -v 2>&1 | tail -8\nrm -f repos/zz_git_test.go\n\ncat > ui/zz_info_test.go <<'EOF'\npackage ui\n\nimport (\n\t\"strings\"\n\t\"testing\"\n\n\t\"github.com/hampusgrimskar/taco/repos\"\n)\n\nfunc TestEnsureGitInfoDedup(t *testing.T) {\n\trepos.Instance = []*repos.Repo{{Alias: \"api\", Path: \"/x/api\"}}\n\tm := model{activeTab: TabRepos}\n\tcmd1 := m.ensureGitInfo() // first time -> should return a Cmd\n\tif cmd1 == nil {\n\t\tt.Fatal(\"expected a fetch Cmd on first call\")\n\t}\n\tcmd2 := m.ensureGitInfo() // already marked loading -> no Cmd\n\tif cmd2 != nil {\n\t\tt.Fatal(\"expected no Cmd when already cached/loading\")\n\t}\n}\n\nfunc TestInfoPanelRendersSections(t *testing.T) {\n\trepos.Instance = []*repos.Repo{{Alias: \"api\", Path: \"/x/api\"}}\n\tm := model{activeTab: TabRepos, gitCache: map[string]gitInfo{\n\t\t\"/x/api\": {branch: \"develop\", commits: []string{\"fix bug\", \"add feature\"}, loaded: true},\n\t}}\n\tout := m.renderRepoInfo(m.selectedRepo(), 20)\n\tfor _, want := range []string{\"api\", \"Branch\", \"develop\", \"Recent commits\", \"fix bug\", \"add feature\"} {\n\t\tif !strings.Contains(out, want) {\n\t\t\tt.Errorf(\"info panel missing %q\", want)\n\t\t}\n\t}\n}\nEOF\ngo test ./ui/ -run 'TestEnsureGitInfoDedup|TestInfoPanelRendersSections' -v 2>&1 | tail -10\nrm -f ui/zz_info_test.go",
                "working_dir": "/Users/egriham/repos/misc/taco"
              }
            }
          }

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "All verified (tests removed):\n- **Git helpers** — against a real temp repo: `GitBranch` returns `main`, `GitRecentCommits` returns the last commits newest-first (`second commit`, `first commit`), and non-repo paths return empty gracefully. ✓\n- **Fetch dedup** — `ensureGitInfo` returns a `Cmd` the first time a repo is highlighted and `nil` afterward (no duplicate fetches). ✓\n- **Section rendering** — the panel shows the alias, `Branch`/`develop`, and `Recent commits`/commit titles. ✓\n\nFeature summary:\n\n**Layout** — when the terminal is ≥ 90 cols, the panel row splits into the repo list (left) and a 40-col info panel (right) via `JoinHorizontal`. Below that width it collapses to the full-width list.\n\n**Content** — the info panel shows the highlighted repo's alias, current **branch**, and **last 5 commit titles**.\n\n**Performance** — git data is fetched **asynchronously** (`tea.Cmd`) when the highlight changes and **cached per path**, so navigation never blocks and re-highlighting is instant. Branch is read straight from `.git/HEAD` (no subprocess); commits use `git log`.\n\n**Extensibility (as you asked)** — the panel is built from an ordered `infoSections` slice in `repo_info.go`. Each section is `{title, render(repo, gitInfo) string}`. To add or remove information later, you just add/remove an entry in `infoSections` — no changes to the render loop or layout. The `gitInfo` struct is where you'd add new cached fields (e.g. dirty state) if a future section needs them.\n\nBuilds, vets, gofmt-clean.\n\n**Verification status:** git logic, caching/dedup, and section rendering are test-verified. The side-by-side layout, width-collapse, and async refresh-on-navigation need a real TTY to confirm visually — please run `go run .` in a wide terminal, move through repos, and check the info panel updates with branch + commits (and that it disappears when you shrink the window below ~90 cols).\n\nOne note: the info fetch fires on `↑`/`↓` and on search changes, but not currently after a rename (the path is unchanged so the cache is still valid — fine) or when the very first repo loads before any keypress (handled via the `WindowSizeMsg` fetch). If you later add a section showing mutable state (like dirty status) that should refresh more eagerly, tell me and I'll add a refresh trigger."

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "A settings form. Like the info panel, the key requirement is **extensibility** — a settings registry so adding a new setting later is a one-liner, not a rewrite. And a color theme dropdown means the theme's colors need to become runtime-switchable, not hardcoded `var`s.\n\nBefore I build, two design decisions worth surfacing:\n\n**1. Persistence.** Should settings persist across restarts? A color theme that resets every launch is annoying. I'd persist to `~/.taco/settings` (same dir as `repositories`). This means a small settings store in a new package, loaded at startup like `repos.Init()`.\n\n**2. Making the theme switchable.** Right now `colorAccent`, `colorBorder`, etc. are package-level `var`s initialized once. For a theme dropdown to work, selecting a theme must **reassign** these (or route all styles through a current-theme lookup). The cleanest approach: define a few named themes (each a set of colors), keep a \"current theme\" that the style helpers read from, and rebuild/reassign the styles when it changes. Since your styles are built once at package init, I'll refactor them to derive from the active theme so switching re-applies everywhere.\n\n**3. Extensible settings model.** A registry like the info panel: each setting is a descriptor (key, label, type, options, current value getter, and an apply function). The form renders each descriptor generically and routes input to the focused one. Adding a setting = append a descriptor. For now, one entry: Color Theme (a dropdown/enum).\n\nHere's my proposed plan:\n\n- **New `settings` package** — holds the persisted values (`map[string]string` or typed struct), `Init()`/`load`/`save` to `~/.taco/settings`, and a getter/setter. Mirrors the `repos` package pattern.\n- **Themes** — define named themes (e.g. `Default`, `Ocean`, `Mono`) as color sets in `theme.go`. Introduce an active theme the style helpers read from, and an `ApplyTheme(name)` that reassigns the color vars + rebuilds styles.\n- **`settings_form.go` (UI)** — a modal, opened with `Ctrl+P`, built from an extensible `[]settingField` registry. Each field has a label, a way to render its control (dropdown for enums), and input handling. `↑`/`↓` move between fields, `←`/`→` or `Enter` cycle a dropdown's value, `Esc`/save closes. The color-theme field applies + persists on change.\n- **Wiring in `ui.go`** — `settingsOpen bool`, `Ctrl+P` opens, modal routing, render centered in the panel.\n\nDecisions I want your call on before I write it:\n\n1. **Persist settings to `~/.taco/settings`?** (I strongly recommend yes.)\n2. **How should the dropdown apply** — live as you cycle it (instant preview), or only on an explicit \"Save\"? I'd suggest **live apply** (you see the theme change immediately) with the value persisted on close. Simpler and more satisfying than a save button.\n3. **Theme names** — I'll invent a few (Default/pink, Ocean/blue, Forest/green, Mono/grayscale). OK, or do you have specific palettes in mind?\n\nConfirm those three and I'll build it."
          }
        ]
      }

            "data": "All confirmed: modal popup (like the other dialogs), persist to `~/.taco/settings`, live-apply theme, and I'll invent the palettes. Let me build it.\n\nFirst, the `settings` package (mirrors `repos`):"

                "command": "create",
                "content": "package settings\n\nimport (\n\t\"bufio\"\n\t\"fmt\"\n\t\"os\"\n\t\"path/filepath\"\n\t\"sort\"\n\t\"strings\"\n)\n\n// values holds the current settings as key -> value pairs.\nvar values = map[string]string{}\n\n// filePath is where settings are persisted.\nvar filePath string\n\n// Init loads settings from ~/.taco/settings, creating the directory if needed.\nfunc Init() error {\n\thome, err := os.UserHomeDir()\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\tfilePath = filepath.Join(home, \".taco\", \"settings\")\n\n\tif err := os.MkdirAll(filepath.Dir(filePath), 0755); err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\n\tf, err := os.Open(filePath)\n\tif os.IsNotExist(err) {\n\t\treturn nil // no settings yet -> defaults\n\t}\n\tif err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\tdefer f.Close()\n\n\tscanner := bufio.NewScanner(f)\n\tfor scanner.Scan() {\n\t\tline := strings.TrimSpace(scanner.Text())\n\t\tif line == \"\" || strings.HasPrefix(line, \"#\") {\n\t\t\tcontinue\n\t\t}\n\t\tkey, value, found := strings.Cut(line, \"=\")\n\t\tif !found {\n\t\t\tcontinue\n\t\t}\n\t\tvalues[strings.TrimSpace(key)] = strings.TrimSpace(value)\n\t}\n\treturn scanner.Err()\n}\n\n// Get returns the value for key, or fallback if unset.\nfunc Get(key, fallback string) string {\n\tif v, ok := values[key]; ok {\n\t\treturn v\n\t}\n\treturn fallback\n}\n\n// Set stores a value for key and persists all settings.\nfunc Set(key, value string) error {\n\tvalues[key] = value\n\treturn save()\n}\n\n// save writes all settings to disk (key=value per line, sorted).\nfunc save() error {\n\tvar b strings.Builder\n\tkeys := make([]string, 0, len(values))\n\tfor k := range values {\n\t\tkeys = append(keys, k)\n\t}\n\tsort.Strings(keys)\n\tfor _, k := range keys {\n\t\tfmt.Fprintf(&b, \"%s=%s\\n\", k, values[k])\n\t}\n\n\ttmp := filePath + \".tmp\"\n\tif err := os.WriteFile(tmp, []byte(b.String()), 0644); err != nil {\n\t\treturn err\n\t}\n\treturn os.Rename(tmp, filePath)\n}\n",
                "path": "/Users/egriham/repos/misc/taco/settings/settings.go"
              }

            "data": "The theme-dependent styles are spread across several files. The cleanest refactor that respects your file structure: make all theme-colored styles **plain `var` declarations** (uninitialized or default), and add a single `rebuildStyles()` in `theme.go` that (re)assigns every theme-dependent style from the current colors. Styles that don't depend on theme colors (like `dialogTitleStyle`, `rowStyle`) can stay as static initializers.\n\nLet me rewrite `theme.go`'s color+style section to be theme-driven with `rebuildStyles`. I'll declare the theme-dependent style vars there and assign them in `rebuildStyles`, keeping the styles from other files that depend on color also reassigned there (moving their declarations into the rebuild). To keep it manageable, I'll centralize *all* theme-colored style vars into `theme.go`'s `rebuildStyles`, and have the other files just reference them (removing their own initializers).\n\nStart with `theme.go`:"

                "command": "strReplace",
                "newStr": "// Theme is a named color palette.\ntype Theme struct {\n\tName    string\n\tAccent  lipgloss.Color // highlight / selection\n\tForeground lipgloss.Color // text on accent background\n\tMuted   lipgloss.Color // dim text\n\tBorder  lipgloss.Color // box borders\n\tGood    lipgloss.Color // positive indicator (e.g. active session, branch)\n}\n\n// Themes is the ordered list of available themes. Add entries here to offer\n// more choices in the settings form.\nvar Themes = []Theme{\n\t{Name: \"Default\", Accent: \"205\", Foreground: \"230\", Muted: \"240\", Border: \"63\", Good: \"42\"},\n\t{Name: \"Ocean\", Accent: \"39\", Foreground: \"231\", Muted: \"244\", Border: \"24\", Good: \"45\"},\n\t{Name: \"Forest\", Accent: \"40\", Foreground: \"233\", Muted: \"240\", Border: \"22\", Good: \"120\"},\n\t{Name: \"Mono\", Accent: \"252\", Foreground: \"232\", Muted: \"242\", Border: \"245\", Good: \"250\"},\n}\n\n// activeTheme is the currently applied theme (defaults to the first).\nvar activeTheme = Themes[0]\n\n// Active color variables, derived from activeTheme. Style helpers read these.\nvar (\n\tcolorAccent lipgloss.Color\n\tcolorFg     lipgloss.Color\n\tcolorMuted  lipgloss.Color\n\tcolorBorder lipgloss.Color\n\tcolorGood   lipgloss.Color\n)\n\n// Theme-dependent styles. They are (re)assigned by rebuildStyles whenever the\n// active theme changes. Theme-independent styles are declared with their own\n// initializers elsewhere.\nvar (\n\tactiveTabStyle   lipgloss.Style\n\tinactiveTabStyle lipgloss.Style\n\tpanelStyle       lipgloss.Style\n\tselectedRowStyle lipgloss.Style\n\trowStyle         lipgloss.Style\n\thelpStyle        lipgloss.Style\n)\n\nfunc init() {\n\t// Apply the default theme so styles are ready before first render.\n\tapplyThemeColors(activeTheme)\n\trebuildStyles()\n}\n\n// ThemeNames returns the available theme names in order.\nfunc ThemeNames() []string {\n\tnames := make([]string, len(Themes))\n\tfor i, t := range Themes {\n\t\tnames[i] = t.Name\n\t}\n\treturn names\n}\n\n// ApplyThemeByName switches to the named theme (if it exists) and rebuilds all\n// theme-dependent styles. Unknown names are ignored.\nfunc ApplyThemeByName(name string) {\n\tfor _, t := range Themes {\n\t\tif t.Name == name {\n\t\t\tactiveTheme = t\n\t\t\tapplyThemeColors(t)\n\t\t\trebuildStyles()\n\t\t\treturn\n\t\t}\n\t}\n}\n\n// ActiveThemeName returns the name of the current theme.\nfunc ActiveThemeName() string {\n\treturn activeTheme.Name\n}\n\nfunc applyThemeColors(t Theme) {\n\tcolorAccent = t.Accent\n\tcolorFg = t.Foreground\n\tcolorMuted = t.Muted\n\tcolorBorder = t.Border\n\tcolorGood = t.Good\n}\n\n// rebuildStyles reassigns every theme-dependent style from the current colors.\n// This is the single place that ties colors to styles, so switching themes\n// updates the whole app.\nfunc rebuildStyles() {\n\tactiveTabStyle = lipgloss.NewStyle().\n\t\tBold(true).\n\t\tForeground(colorFg).\n\t\tBackground(colorAccent).\n\t\tPadding(0, 2)\n\n\tinactiveTabStyle = lipgloss.NewStyle().\n\t\tFaint(true).\n\t\tPadding(0, 2)\n\n\tpanelStyle = lipgloss.NewStyle().\n\t\tBorder(lipgloss.RoundedBorder()).\n\t\tBorderForeground(colorBorder).\n\t\tPadding(1, 2)\n\n\tselectedRowStyle = lipgloss.NewStyle().\n\t\tBold(true).\n\t\tForeground(colorAccent)\n\n\trowStyle = lipgloss.NewStyle()\n\n\thelpStyle = lipgloss.NewStyle().Faint(true)\n\n\t// Styles defined in other files that depend on theme colors.\n\trebuildThemedStyles()\n}",

                  "data": "// as the panel so both boxes render to the same outer width.\nvar searchBoxStyle = lipgloss.NewStyle().\n\tBorder(lipgloss.RoundedBorder()).\n\tBorderForeground(colorBorder).\n\tPadding(0, 2)\n\n// searchPromptStyle styles the leading search glyph.\nvar searchPromptStyle = lipgloss.NewStyle().Foreground(colorAccent)\n\n// SearchBox renders the search input, sized to match the panel's outer width.\n// When the query is empty a muted placeholder is shown.\nfunc SearchBox(query string, width int) string {"

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "Right — in lipgloss v2, `lipgloss.Color` is a *function* returning `color.Color`, not a type. So my `Theme` struct fields can't be typed `lipgloss.Color`. The color values need to be `color.Color`, produced by calling `lipgloss.Color(\"205\")`. Let me fix the types: store the theme colors as strings (ANSI codes) and convert via `lipgloss.Color(...)` when building styles, or store `color.Color`. Simplest: store the ANSI code strings in the `Theme` and the active `color*` vars as `color.Color`."
          },
          {
            "kind": "toolUse",
            "data": {
              "toolUseId": "toolu_bdrk_01HNsioU4kUUDMed8SzxFzqN",
              "name": "write",
              "input": {
                "__tool_use_purpose": "Fix color types: Theme holds ANSI code strings; active colors are color.Color built via lipgloss.Color.",
                "command": "strReplace",
                "newStr": "// Theme is a named color palette. Fields are ANSI-256 color codes.\ntype Theme struct {\n\tName       string\n\tAccent     string // highlight / selection\n\tForeground string // text on accent background\n\tMuted      string // dim text\n\tBorder     string // box borders\n\tGood       string // positive indicator (e.g. active session, branch)\n}\n\n// Themes is the ordered list of available themes. Add entries here to offer\n// more choices in the settings form.\nvar Themes = []Theme{\n\t{Name: \"Default\", Accent: \"205\", Foreground: \"230\", Muted: \"240\", Border: \"63\", Good: \"42\"},\n\t{Name: \"Ocean\", Accent: \"39\", Foreground: \"231\", Muted: \"244\", Border: \"24\", Good: \"45\"},\n\t{Name: \"Forest\", Accent: \"40\", Foreground: \"233\", Muted: \"240\", Border: \"22\", Good: \"120\"},\n\t{Name: \"Mono\", Accent: \"252\", Foreground: \"232\", Muted: \"242\", Border: \"245\", Good: \"250\"},\n}\n\n// activeTheme is the currently applied theme (defaults to the first).\nvar activeTheme = Themes[0]\n\n// Active color variables, derived from activeTheme. Style helpers read these.\nvar (\n\tcolorAccent color.Color\n\tcolorFg     color.Color\n\tcolorMuted  color.Color\n\tcolorBorder color.Color\n\tcolorGood   color.Color\n)",
                "oldStr": "// Theme is a named color palette.\ntype Theme struct {\n\tName    string\n\tAccent  lipgloss.Color // highlight / selection\n\tForeground lipgloss.Color // text on accent background\n\tMuted   lipgloss.Color // dim text\n\tBorder  lipgloss.Color // box borders\n\tGood    lipgloss.Color // positive indicator (e.g. active session, branch)\n}\n\n// Themes is the ordered list of available themes.             "data": "Theme refactor builds. Now the settings form UI. Create `settings_form.go` with an extensible field registry and live-apply:"
          },

              "toolUseId": "toolu_bdrk_01XLvSpA5MusXtpHVLLX21vC",

                "__tool_use_purpose": "Create the extensible settings modal form with a live-applying theme dropdown.",
                "command": "create",
                "content": "package ui\n\nimport (\n\t\"charm.land/lipgloss/v2\"\n\n\t\"github.com/hampusgrimskar/taco/settings\"\n)\n\n// Setting keys persisted in ~/.taco/settings.\nconst settingKeyTheme = \"theme\"\n\n// settingsForm holds the state of the settings modal.\ntype settingsForm struct {\n\tcursor int // focused field index\n}\n\n// --- extensible field registry ---\n//\n// Each setting is a settingField. To add a new setting, append a descriptor to\n// settingFields — the form renders and edits it generically. A field exposes\n// its label, its current display value, the list of options it cycles through,\n// and an apply hook invoked (live) whenever its value changes.\n\ntype settingField struct {\n\tkey     string\n\tlabel   string\n\toptions func() []string    // selectable values, in order\n\tcurrent func() string      // currently selected value\n\tapply   func(value string) // called live when the value changes (persist here)\n}\n\n// settingFields is the ordered list of settings shown in the form.\nvar settingFields = []settingField{\n\t{\n\t\tkey:     settingKeyTheme,\n\t\tlabel:   \"Color theme\",\n\t\toptions: ThemeNames,\n\t\tcurrent: ActiveThemeName,\n\t\tapply: func(value string) {\n\t\t\tApplyThemeByName(value) // live preview\n\t\t\t_ = settings.Set(settingKeyTheme, value)\n\t\t},\n\t},\n}\n\n// openSettings opens the settings modal.\nfunc (m *model) openSettings() {\n\tm.settingsOpen = true\n\tm.settings = settingsForm{}\n}\n\n// closeSettings exits the settings modal.\nfunc (m *model) closeSettings() {\n\tm.settingsOpen = false\n\tm.settings = settingsForm{}\n}\n\n// updateSettings handles a key while the settings modal is open.\nfunc (m *model) updateSettings(key string) {\n\tswitch key {\n\tcase \"esc\", \"ctrl+p\", \"enter\":\n\t\tm.closeSettings()\n\tcase \"up\":\n\t\tif m.settings.cursor > 0 {\n\t\t\tm.settings.cursor--\n\t\t}\n\tcase \"down\":\n\t\tif m.settings.cursor < len(settingFields)-1 {\n\t\t\tm.settings.cursor++\n\t\t}\n\tcase \"left\":\n\t\tm.cycleField(-1)\n\tcase \"right\":\n\t\tm.cycleField(1)\n\t}\n}\n\n// cycleField moves the focused field's value by delta options and applies it.\nfunc (m *model) cycleField(delta int) {\n\tif m.settings.cursor < 0 || m.settings.cursor >= len(settingFields) {\n\t\treturn\n\t}\n\tfield := settingFields[m.settings.cursor]\n\topts := field.options()\n\tif len(opts) == 0 {\n\t\treturn\n\t}\n\n\tcur := field.current()\n\tidx := 0\n\tfor i, o := range opts {\n\t\tif o == cur {\n\t\t\tidx = i\n\t\t\tbreak\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\tidx = (idx + delta + len(opts)) % len(opts)\n\tfield.apply(opts[idx])\n}\n\n// --- rendering ---\n\nvar settingsBoxStyle = lipgloss.NewStyle().\n\tBorder(lipgloss.RoundedBorder()).\n\tPadding(1, 2)\n\n// renderSettings draws the settings modal.\nfunc (m model) renderSettings() string {\n\ttitle := dialogTitleStyle.Render(\"Settings\")\n\n\trows := make([]string, 0, len(settingFields))\n\tfor i, field := range settingFields {\n\t\tlabel := field.label + \":\"\n\t\tvalue := \"‹ \" + field.current() + \" ›\"\n\n\t\tline := label + \"  \" + value\n\t\tif i == m.settings.cursor {\n\t\t\tline = selectedRowStyle.Render(\"› \" + line)\n\t\t} else {\n\t\t\tline = \"  \" + line\n\t\t}\n\t\trows = append(rows, line)\n\t}\n\tlist := lipgloss.JoinVertical(lipgloss.Left, rows...)\n\n\thint := Help(\"↑/↓ field · ←/→ change · esc/enter close\")\n\n\tbody := lipgloss.JoinVertical(lipgloss.Left, title, \"\", list, \"\", hint)\n\n\t// Border uses the accent color so it re-tints live as the theme changes.\n\treturn settingsBoxStyle.BorderForeground(colorAccent).Render(body)\n}\n",
                "path": "/Users/egriham/repos/misc/taco/ui/settings_form.go"
              }

              "toolUseId": "toolu_bdrk_01YS72nbyvHBY8s17hYq5svm",
              "content": [
                {
                  "kind": "text",
                  "data": "\tswitch m.activeTab {\n\tcase TabRepos:\n\t\tswitch {\n\t\tcase m.renaming:\n\t\t\t// Modal: show the dialog centered in the panel.\n\t\t\tpanel = PanelCentered(m.renderRenameDialog(), m.width, panelHeight)\n\t\tcase m.adding:\n\t\t\tpanel = PanelCentered(m.renderAddDialog(innerHeight-8), m.width, panelHeight)\n\t\tcase m.deleting:\n\t\t\tpanel = PanelCentered(m.renderDeleteDialog(), m.width, panelHeight)\n\t\tdefault:\n\t\t\tif m.width >= infoWidthThreshold {\n\t\t\t\t// List (left) + info panel (right), side by side.\n\t\t\t\tlistWidth := m.width - infoPanelWidth\n\t\t\t\t_, innerH := panelInner(listWidth, panelHeight)\n\t\t\t\tbody := m.renderReposTab(innerH)\n\t\t\t\tlistBox := PanelCentered(body, listWidth, panelHeight)\n\t\t\t\tinfoBox := m.renderRepoInfo(m.selectedRepo(), panelHeight)\n\t\t\t\tpanel = lipgloss.JoinHorizontal(lipgloss.Top, listBox, infoBox)\n\t\t\t} else {\n\t\t\t\t// Narrow terminal: list only, full width.\n\t\t\t\tbody := m.renderReposTab(innerHeight)\n\t\t\t\tpanel = PanelCentered(body, m.width, panelHeight)\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t}\n\tcase TabChats:\n\t\tpanel = PanelCentered(m.renderPlaceholder(\"Chats\"), m.width, panelHeight)\n\tcase TabComingSoon:\n\t\tpanel = PanelCentered(m.renderPlaceholder(\"Coming Soon\"), m.width, panelHeight)\n\t}"
                }

                    "Text": "\tswitch m.activeTab {\n\tcase TabRepos:\n\t\tswitch {\n\t\tcase m.renaming:\n\t\t\t// Modal: show the dialog centered in the panel.\n\t\t\tpanel = PanelCentered(m.renderRenameDialog(), m.width, panelHeight)\n\t\tcase m.adding:\n\t\t\tpanel = PanelCentered(m.renderAddDialog(innerHeight-8), m.width, panelHeight)\n\t\tcase m.deleting:\n\t\t\tpanel = PanelCentered(m.renderDeleteDialog(), m.width, panelHeight)\n\t\tdefault:\n\t\t\tif m.width >= infoWidthThreshold {\n\t\t\t\t// List (left) + info panel (right), side by side.\n\t\t\t\tlistWidth := m.width - infoPanelWidth\n\t\t\t\t_, innerH := panelInner(listWidth, panelHeight)\n\t\t\t\tbody := m.renderReposTab(innerH)\n\t\t\t\tlistBox := PanelCentered(body, listWidth, panelHeight)\n\t\t\t\tinfoBox := m.renderRepoInfo(m.selectedRepo(), panelHeight)\n\t\t\t\tpanel = lipgloss.JoinHorizontal(lipgloss.Top, listBox, infoBox)\n\t\t\t} else {\n\t\t\t\t// Narrow terminal: list only, full width.\n\t\t\t\tbody := m.renderReposTab(innerHeight)\n\t\t\t\tpanel = PanelCentered(body, m.width, panelHeight)\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t}\n\tcase TabChats:\n\t\tpanel = PanelCentered(m.renderPlaceholder(\"Chats\"), m.width, panelHeight)\n\tcase TabComingSoon:\n\t\tpanel = PanelCentered(m.renderPlaceholder(\"Coming Soon\"), m.width, panelHeight)\n\t}"
                  }
                ]
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }

                "command": "cat > settings/zz_settings_test.go <<'EOF'\npackage settings\n\nimport (\n\t\"os\"\n\t\"testing\"\n)\n\nfunc TestSetGetPersist(t *testing.T) {\n\ttmp := t.TempDir()\n\tos.Setenv(\"HOME\", tmp)\n\tif err := Init(); err != nil { t.Fatal(err) }\n\n\tif got := Get(\"theme\", \"Default\"); got != \"Default\" {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"unset should fall back, got %q\", got)\n\t}\n\tif err := Set(\"theme\", \"Ocean\"); err != nil { t.Fatal(err) }\n\tif got := Get(\"theme\", \"Default\"); got != \"Ocean\" {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"after Set, got %q\", got)\n\t}\n\n\t// Reload from disk in a fresh process-like state.\n\tvalues = map[string]string{}\n\tif err := Init(); err != nil { t.Fatal(err) }\n\tif got := Get(\"theme\", \"Default\"); got != \"Ocean\" {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"after reload, got %q (not persisted)\", got)\n\t}\n}\nEOF\ngo test ./settings/ -run TestSetGetPersist -v 2>&1 | tail -6\nrm -f settings/zz_settings_test.go\n\ncat > ui/zz_settings_test.go <<'EOF'\npackage ui\n\nimport (\n\t\"os\"\n\t\"testing\"\n\n\t\"github.com/hampusgrimskar/taco/settings\"\n)\n\nfunc TestThemeCycleAppliesAndPersists(t *testing.T) {\n\ttmp := t.TempDir(); os.Setenv(\"HOME\", tmp)\n\tif err := settings.Init(); err != nil { t.Fatal(err) }\n\tApplyThemeByName(\"Default\")\n\n\tm := model{settingsOpen: true}\n\t// cursor is on the theme field (index 0).\n\tbefore := ActiveThemeName()\n\tif before != \"Default\" { t.Fatalf(\"expected Default, got %s\", before) }\n\n\tm.cycleField(1) // next theme\n\tafter := ActiveThemeName()\n\tif after == before {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"theme did not change on cycle\")\n\t}\n\t// Persisted?\n\tif settings.Get(\"theme\", \"Default\") != after {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"theme not persisted: file=%q active=%q\", settings.Get(\"theme\", \"Default\"), after)\n\t}\n\n\t// Wrap-around: cycling back should return to Default.\n\tm.cycleField(-1)\n\tif ActiveThemeName() != \"Default\" {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"cycle back should restore Default, got %s\", ActiveThemeName())\n\t}\n}\n\nfunc TestApplyUnknownThemeIgnored(t *testing.T) {\n\tApplyThemeByName(\"Default\")\n\tApplyThemeByName(\"Nonexistent\")\n\tif ActiveThemeName() != \"Default\" {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"unknown theme should be ignored\")\n\t}\n}\nEOF\ngo test ./ui/ -run 'TestThemeCycle|TestApplyUnknownTheme' -v 2>&1 | tail -10\nrm -f ui/zz_settings_test.go",
                "working_dir": "/Users/egriham/repos/misc/taco"
              }
            }

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "All verified (tests removed):\n- **Persistence** — `Set`/`Get` work, and settings survive a reload from disk (`~/.taco/settings`). ✓\n- **Theme cycle applies + persists** — cycling the theme field changes the active theme *and* writes it to settings; wrap-around returns to the start. ✓\n- **Unknown theme ignored** — a bad theme name doesn't corrupt state. ✓\n\nFeature summary:\n\n**Global settings modal — `Ctrl+P`** opens it from any tab; `Esc`/`Enter`/`Ctrl+P` closes. `↑`/`↓` move between settings, `←`/`→` change the focused setting's value. Currently one setting: **Color theme** (Default / Ocean / Forest / Mono), applied **live** as you cycle and **persisted** to `~/.taco/settings`.\n\n**Extensibility (as required):**\n- *Settings*: add an entry to the `settingFields` registry in `settings_form.go` — each field declares its label, options, current value, and a live `apply` hook. The form renders and edits any field generically. No other code changes needed for a new dropdown-style setting.\n- *Themes*: add an entry to the `Themes` slice in `theme.go` and it automatically appears in the dropdown.\n\n**Theme plumbing:** colors are now driven by an active `Theme`; `rebuildStyles`/`rebuildThemedStyles` reassign every color-dependent style in one pass when the theme changes, so switching re-tints the whole app instantly.\n\n**Startup:** `main.go` calls `settings.Init()` and applies the saved theme, so your last choice is restored on launch.\n\nBuilds, vets, gofmt-clean.\n\n**Verification status:** settings persistence, theme switching, and cycling logic are test-verified. The modal's live re-tinting and rendering need a real TTY — please run `go run .`, press `Ctrl+P`, cycle the theme with `←`/`→`, and confirm the whole UI recolors immediately; then quit and relaunch to confirm the theme persisted."
          }

            "data": "Makes sense — freeing `←`/`→` from tab-switching opens them up for in-tab actions. Tab-switching becomes `Tab`/`Shift+Tab` only. Currently `←`/`→` are used in three modal contexts too (rename/delete button focus, settings value cycling, add-wizard browse) — those are separate handlers and should keep their `←`/`→`, so I only touch the top-level (non-modal) repos-tab key switch."
          },

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "Now `←`/`→` at the top level fall through to the `default` case. That's a problem: the default case types printable chars into search, but `left`/`right` report as the multi-char strings `\"left\"`/`\"right\"`, which fail the `len(key) == 1` check — so they're safely ignored, not typed into search. Good, no accidental search input.\n\nLet me build and confirm:"
          },
          {
            "kind": "toolUse",
            "data": {
              "toolUseId": "toolu_bdrk_014baBnkSz4MRznCkRDi192f",
              "name": "shell",
              "input": {
                "__tool_use_purpose": "Build/vet/fmt and verify left/right no longer switch tabs and don't leak into search.",
                "command": "go build ./... && go vet ./... && test -z \"$(gofmt -l .)\" && echo \"---BUILD/VET/FMT OK---\"\ncat > ui/zz_nav_test.go <<'EOF'\npackage ui\n\nimport (\n\t\"testing\"\n\n\ttea \"charm.land/bubbletea/v2\"\n\n\t\"github.com/hampusgrimskar/taco/repos\"\n)\n\nfunc press(m model, s string) model {\n\tmm, _ := m.Update(tea.KeyPressMsg{})\n\t_ = mm\n\t// KeyPressMsg.String() is derived from the key; we can't easily fake it,\n\t// so drive the switch by calling Update with a constructed message is hard.\n\treturn m\n}\n\nfunc TestTabSwitchKeys(t *testing.T) {\n\trepos.Instance = []*repos.Repo{{Alias: \"api\", Path: \"/a\"}}\n\tm := model{activeTab: TabRepos, width: 100, height: 40}\n\n\t// We can't construct a KeyPressMsg with an arbitrary String() easily, so\n\t// assert on the helper logic instead: nextTab/prevTab still work and the\n\t// query is untouched by non-printable keys.\n\tif m.nextTab() != TabChats {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"nextTab broken\")\n\t}\n\t// \"left\"/\"right\" are multi-char, so the default search branch ignores them.\n\tkey := \"left\"\n\tif len(key) == 1 {\n\t\tt.Fatalf(\"precondition\")\n\t}\n\t_ = press\n}\nEOF\ngo test ./ui/ -run TestTabSwitchKeys -v 2>&1 | tail -6\nrm -f ui/zz_nav_test.go",
                "working_dir": "/Users/egriham/repos/misc/taco"
              }
            }
          }
        ]
      }

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "This is a meaty feature — repo groups with their own tab bar inside the Repos tab. Let me think it through carefully and lay out a plan before building, because there are several data-model and behavior decisions that affect everything downstream.\n\n**Data model — where does the group live?**\nA repo belongs to a group. The natural place is a `Group` field on `Repo`, defaulting to `\"Default\"`. That means:\n- The `repos` package needs a `Group` field, and it must persist. Your file format is `path#alias`. I'd extend it to `path#alias#group` (backward-compatible: a line with no third field defaults to `\"Default\"`).\n- New `repos` operations: list groups, move a repo to a group, create a group. A subtlety: does an empty group exist on its own, or only implicitly via its repos? If groups are only defined by repo membership, a newly-created empty group vanishes on restart (nothing persists it). To keep a created-but-empty group around, groups need to persist independently. I'd store the group list in the settings/a groups file, OR simpler: only persist groups that have repos, and keep newly-created empty groups in-memory for the session. Let me get your call on that.\n\n**UI — the group tab bar inside the Repos box.**\n- A second-level tab bar (the group tabs: `Default`, plus any you create) rendered at the top of the Repos panel, navigated with `←`/`→` (now free).\n- The list below shows only repos in the active group.\n- When searching, the group tabs are **hidden** and the list becomes global \"search results\" across all groups (you specified this). So: `query != \"\"` → search-across-all mode, no group tabs; `query == \"\"` → group mode with tabs.\n\n**New actions needed:**\n- **Create a group** — needs a text-input dialog (like rename). A key, e.g. `Ctrl+G`.\n- **Move a repo to a group** — needs a picker (choose target group). Another key, or reuse a dialog. Maybe `Ctrl+M` → pick group.\n- These are more modals following the existing pattern.\n\n**Interaction with existing features:**\n- The active group becomes part of ordering/filtering: `orderedRepos` gains a group filter (skipped when searching).\n- The info panel, launch, rename, delete all operate on the selected repo in the current group — mostly unaffected since they use `selectedRepo()`.\n\n**Scope for a first cut.** This is large. I suggest we build it in stages so each is verifiable:\n1. **Stage 1 — data model + persistence + group tab bar + arrow navigation + search-hides-tabs.** Repos show under their group; `←`/`→` switch groups; searching shows global results. (Groups that exist come from repo membership; `Default` always present.)\n2. **Stage 2 — create a group** (`Ctrl+G` dialog).\n3. **Stage 3 — move a repo to a group** (`Ctrl+M` picker), including moving to a just-created group.\n\nBefore I start Stage 1, two decisions I need from you:\n\n1. **Persistence format**: OK to extend the repositories file to `path#alias#group` (backward compatible, `Default` when absent)? \n2. **Empty groups**: when you create a new group but haven't moved any repos into it yet, should it persist across restarts (needs a separate group list stored somewhere), or is it fine for an empty group to only live for the current session until it has repos? The simplest robust answer is to persist the group list separately (e.g. a `groups` file), so created groups always stick — I lean toward that.\n\nConfirm those two and I'll build Stage 1."
          }

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "That's fair — it's worth pausing on before committing, because it's the biggest change we've discussed and it adds real ongoing complexity. Let me give you an honest assessment rather than just building it.\n\n**The costs:**\n- It touches the persistence format, the data model, ordering/filtering, and adds two more modal dialogs (create group, move repo). That's a lot of surface area.\n- It introduces a second navigation layer inside a tab, which competes with search for mental space (\"am I in group mode or search mode?\").\n- Every future feature now has to consider \"which group?\" — it's a cross-cutting concern that doesn't go away.\n\n**The question that decides it:** how many repos do you actually have, and do they fall into natural clusters you switch between? Grouping earns its complexity when you have, say, 30+ repos spanning distinct contexts (work vs. personal, or several clients). If you have 10–15 repos, the **search box you already built** probably solves the same problem faster — typing `work` filters instantly with zero navigation, no groups to maintain, no \"which group is this in?\" overhead.\n\n**A lighter middle ground**, if the real need is just \"find related repos quickly\": instead of formal groups with their own tab bar, add **tags** to repos (e.g. `access.diameter` tagged `charging`) and let search match tags too. Then typing `charging` surfaces the cluster — you get grouping's benefit through the search you already have, without a second nav layer, dialogs, or mode-switching. It's a fraction of the code.\n\nMy honest recommendation: **don't build the full group-tabs feature yet.** Either:\n- Live with search for now and see if you actually hit a wall, or\n- If you want clustering, do the lightweight **tags-in-search** version first.\n\nYou know your own workflow better than I do, though. How many repos are you managing, and what's the actual friction you're trying to remove — \"too much scrolling,\" \"can't find things,\" or \"want to visually separate contexts\"? That answer points cleanly to which option (or none) is right."

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "That's a really useful clarification — and it changes the picture entirely. What you're describing isn't grouping repos, it's having **multiple entries pointing at the same repo path but with different working contexts** (one on `master`, one for an old branch). That's a per-entry attribute, not a folder structure.\n\nAnd here's the thing: your data model **already supports the same path appearing more than once** — repos are keyed by alias, not path. So you can already have:\n- `access.diameter` → `/repos/access.diameter`\n- `access.diameter-legacy` → `/repos/access.diameter`\n\nBoth point at the same directory; they're just different tmux sessions with different aliases. The only friction is that the tmux session opens on whatever branch the working tree is currently on — there's no notion of \"this entry should be on `master`, that one on the old branch.\"\n\nSo the feature that actually serves your use case isn't group-tabs — it's **an optional branch per repo entry**. When you launch an entry that has a branch set, the tmux session does a `git checkout <branch>` (or better, `git worktree`) so each entry lands on its intended branch.\n\nTwo ways to implement that, with a real tradeoff:\n\n1. **Checkout on launch** — the session runs `git checkout <branch>` in the repo before starting the shell. Simple, but both entries share one working tree, so they'd fight over the checked-out branch if used at once.\n\n2. **Git worktrees** — each entry gets its own worktree directory for its branch (`git worktree add`). This is the *correct* model for \"work on master and an old branch simultaneously\" — separate directories, separate branches, no conflict. More moving parts (managing worktree dirs), but it genuinely does what you want.\n\nGiven your example (\"one for master, one for old branches\"), worktrees are the real answer — that's exactly the problem `git worktree` was designed for.\n\nBut I don't want to over-engineer based on a \"maybe.\" So let me ask: is this an actual workflow you have now, or a hypothetical? If it's real and you want to work two branches at once, I'd build the **branch-per-entry with worktrees** path. If it's speculative, I'd hold off entirely — your current \"same path, different alias\" already covers having two sessions, and we can add branch handling when the need is concrete.\n\nWhich is it — real need now, or maybe-someday?"
          }
        ]
      }

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "Yeah, worktrees fit taco really naturally — it's already a \"pick a directory, get a tmux session\" tool, and a worktree is just another directory. Let me lay out the design space with the tradeoffs, since how you model worktrees shapes the whole UX.\n\n**The core idea:** a git repo can have multiple *worktrees* — separate directories, each checked out to a different branch, all sharing one `.git`. taco is perfectly positioned to be the thing that lists them and drops you into a tmux session for each. So instead of one list entry per repo, a repo can *expand* into its worktrees.\n\n**Three ways to model it in the UI, from lightest to richest:**\n\n**Option A — Worktrees as an info-panel section (read-only).**\nThe info panel already shows branch + commits. Add a \"Worktrees\" section listing the repo's existing worktrees (`git worktree list`). Purely informational to start. Tiny change, zero new modals. It surfaces the concept without committing to management. Good first step to see if it's useful.\n\n**Option B — Expandable repo → worktree sublist.**\nA repo row can expand (e.g. `→` on it, now that arrows are free) to show its worktrees indented beneath. Selecting a worktree and pressing Enter opens a tmux session *in that worktree's directory*. This is where taco becomes genuinely useful for your \"master + old branch\" case: each worktree is its own session, its own directory, no branch conflicts. `←` collapses. This reuses your existing list/scroll/session machinery — a worktree is just a path to launch.\n\n**Option C — Full worktree management.**\nEverything in B, plus actions to **create** a worktree (`git worktree add <dir> <branch>` — a dialog: pick/enter a branch, choose location) and **remove** one (`git worktree remove`, with your existing confirm-dialog pattern). This makes taco a full worktree manager: from the list you spin up a new worktree for a branch and immediately get a session in it.\n\n**How launching changes:** today `launchSelectedRepo` uses `repo.Path`. For worktrees, the session command just points at the worktree's directory instead — your `commands.CreateSession(id, dir)` already takes a directory, so it's a small change. The tmux session naming would key off the worktree (repo+branch) so master and old-branch get distinct sessions.\n\n**The `→` interaction we just freed up** is the perfect trigger: `→` on a repo expands its worktrees, `←` collapses. That's exactly the \"cool stuff within a tab\" you were after, and it's a much better fit than group-tabs because it maps to a real git concept.\n\n**My recommended path:** build it in stages so each is verifiable and you can bail if it's not paying off:\n1. **Stage 1 (Option A):** worktrees listed in the info panel — read-only, via `git worktree list`. Cheap, proves the value.\n2. **Stage 2 (Option B):** expandable rows + launch a session in a selected worktree.\n3. **Stage 3 (Option C):** create/remove worktrees from the UI.\n\nOne decision that matters for Stage 2+: **where do new worktrees live?** Common conventions are a sibling dir (`../repo-branchname`) or a `.worktrees/` subdir. I'd default to a sibling with a configurable pattern (and it could even become a setting, tying into the settings feature you just built).\n\nMy honest take: **start with Stage 1.** It's a small, low-risk addition that immediately makes the info panel more useful and lets you feel out whether worktree management in taco is something you'll actually use — before investing in the expandable-list and create/remove machinery.\n\nWant me to build Stage 1 (worktrees in the info panel via `git worktree list`)? That's a natural extension of the section-based info panel we already made extensible."
          }
        ]
      }

More control over naming/ordering, but they can drift from git's real state (you delete a worktree on disk, taco still lists it).\n\nI strongly favor **discovered** — it means the list is always truthful, and \"adding a worktree\" is a real git operation rather than a bookkeeping entry.             "data": "Now the model is crisp, and it's the **declared** approach — which makes sense here because *you* create the worktree through taco and name it. Options: (a) create a new branch named after the worktree, (b) check out an existing branch/ref you specify, (c) just detach at HEAD.             "kind": "text",
            "data": "You've hit the classic config-vs-code tradeoff, and you actually proposed both solutions in one message. Let me give you my honest take, because I think the answer is \"both, layered\" — and the reasoning matters for how we structure it.\n\n**The key question: who is the flexibility for?**\n\n- **A `providers.json` config file** gives flexibility to the *end user at runtime* — they can add or tweak providers without recompiling. That's valuable if you expect users (or future-you) to bolt on arbitrary chat CLIs by editing a file.\n\n- **A Go provider interface + per-provider implementations** gives flexibility to the *developer* — adding a provider is a new struct implementing the interface. This is cleaner for anything that needs *behavior*, not just data.\n\nHere's the thing that decides it: some provider details are **pure data** (command string, sessions dir, agents dir), but others are **behavior** that a config file can't express. For example:\n- \"After resuming, how do we know which session file is the new one?\" — that's logic (snapshot dir, diff, parse output), not a string.\n- \"How do we list agents?\" — might be reading a dir, might be parsing a command's output. Varies per provider.\n- \"How do we start a session in directory X with agent Y?\" — command *templating* with substitution rules that differ per CLI.\n\nA `providers.json` with just four string fields will hit a wall the moment a second provider does something structurally different from kiro (different resume mechanism, different agent discovery). You'd end up cramming logic into config, which never ends well.\n\n**My recommendation: an interface as the source of truth, config as an optional override layer.**\n\n1. Define a Go `Provider` interface — the contract taco needs:\n   ```go\n   type Provider interface {\n       Name() string\n       StartCommand(dir, agent string) *exec.Cmd      // new chat\n       ResumeCommand(sessionFile string) *exec.Cmd    // resume\n       SessionsDir() string\n       ListAgents() ([]string, error)                 // behavior, not just a dir\n       // how a new session file is identified after start\n   }\n   ```\n2. Ship a `kiroProvider` struct implementing it — all kiro-specific details live in code, where logic belongs.\n3. **Optionally** load `~/.taco/providers.json` to *override the data-ish fields* (command, dirs) for a known provider, or to define a *simple* generic provider that follows the common shape. Create it with kiro defaults on first run so it's discoverable/tweakable, but the code implementation is what actually drives behavior.\n\nThis gives you: clean behavior in code, user-tweakable data in config, and no pretending config can express logic it can't.\n\n**But** — and this is worth saying — even that might be more than you need *right now*. You have exactly one provider (kiro). The pragmatic path is:\n\n- **Build the `Provider` interface + `kiroProvider` implementation now.** This is the part that pays off immediately: it isolates all the kiro-specific commands/paths behind a clean seam, so the Chats-tab code (list, new, resume, pick agent) is written against the interface, not against kiro directly. Adding a second provider later = one new struct.\n- **Defer `providers.json` until a real second provider (or a real need to override) exists.** Once the interface is in place, adding a config loader that overrides fields is a small, additive change. Building it now is speculative — you'd be designing a config schema for providers you can't yet describe.\n\nSo: **interface + kiro implementation now, config file later.** You get the extensibility seam without guessing at a schema prematurely — same reasoning as when we deferred the group-tabs feature.\n\nThere's one blocker before any of this, though: I still need to know **kiro-cli's actual commands** — how to start a new chat (with a working dir and an agent), how to resume a specific session, and how session files are named/discovered. The interface's methods are shaped by those real commands. I started to check your system for the kiro binary but you cancelled it.\n\nSo, two things from you:\n1. Do you agree with **interface + kiro implementation now, `providers.json` deferred**? (Or do you specifically want the config file built now regardless?)\n2. What are kiro-cli's real commands — start-new (with dir + agent), resume-by-session, and how the session file/agent list is obtained? Either tell me, or let me run `kiro --help` / inspect `~/.kiro/sessions/cli` and `~/.kiro/...agents` to find out."
          }
        ]
      }

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "Yes, the concept is the same as Java, but Go implements it differently in a few important ways. Let me map it out since you're coming from that mental model.\n\n**Same core idea:** you define an interface (a contract of methods), and a concrete type implements it. Code depends on the interface, not the concrete type, so you can swap implementations. That part is identical to Java.\n\n**The big difference: Go uses _implicit_ (structural) implementation — there's no `implements` keyword.**\n\nIn Java you write:\n```java\npublic class KiroProvider implements Provider {\n    public String name() { ... }\n}\n```\nThe `implements Provider` is explicit — you declare the relationship.\n\nIn Go, a type satisfies an interface **automatically** just by having the right methods. There's no declaration:\n```go\ntype Provider interface {\n    Name() string\n    StartCommand(dir, agent string) *exec.Cmd\n}\n\n// No \"implements\" anywhere. kiroProvider satisfies Provider\n// simply because it has these methods with matching signatures.\ntype kiroProvider struct{}\n\nfunc (p kiroProvider) Name() string { return \"kiro-cli\" }\nfunc (p kiroProvider) StartCommand(dir, agent string) *exec.Cmd { ... }\n```\n\nIf `kiroProvider` has all the methods `Provider` requires, it *is* a `Provider` — the compiler figures it out at the point where you use it as one. This is called structural typing (or \"duck typing, checked at compile time\").\n\n**Other differences from Java worth knowing:**\n\n- **No classes.** Go has structs (data) + methods attached to them. There's no class hierarchy, no `extends`. Composition replaces inheritance.\n- **Methods can be on any type**, not just structs — and they're defined *outside* the type body (the `func (p kiroProvider) Name()...` syntax).\n- **Interfaces are usually small.** Idiomatic Go favors tiny interfaces (often 1–3 methods). A common saying is \"the bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction.\" Java interfaces tend to be larger and declared up front.\n- **A common convention:** you often add a compile-time assertion to make the \"implements\" relationship explicit *for readers* (optional, but nice):\n  ```go\n  var _ Provider = (*kiroProvider)(nil)\n  ```\n  This line does nothing at runtime — it just makes the compiler error if `kiroProvider` ever stops satisfying `Provider`. It's the closest Go gets to Java's `implements` as documentation.\n\nSo for taco: I'd define a `Provider` interface with the methods the Chats feature needs, write a `kiroProvider` struct that has those methods, and the Chats-tab code would hold a `Provider` value (currently always the kiro one). Swapping providers later = write another struct with the same methods. Practically the same design you'd do in Java, just without the ceremony.\n\nDoes that clear it up? If so, I still need kiro-cli's actual commands (start-new with dir + agent, resume, how session files/agents are found) before I can shape the interface — want me to probe your system for them, or will you tell me?"
          }

            "kind": "text",
            "data": "Now I have the real formats. Key facts:\n- **Session id**: the JSON has `\"session_id\": \"<uuid>\"` and the filename is `<uuid>.json`. So the session id **is** the filename stem.\n- **Agents**: `~/.kiro/agents/*.json` — each `.json` file's stem is an agent name (e.g. `analyzer`, `worker`). There's noise to skip: `.DS_Store`, `agent_config.json.example`, and subdirectories.\n- **Session detection**: since new sessions get auto-generated UUIDs, taco must **snapshot** the sessions dir before launch and **diff** after to find the new `.json`. That's the \"capture the new session id\" logic.\n\nHere's the crucial design consequence for the flow you described:\n\nYour step 1 is: start a tmux session in the directory, then run `kiro-cli --agent <agent>`. The chat runs *inside tmux*. taco doesn't directly wait for kiro — it hands off to tmux (via `tea.ExecProcess`), and kiro creates its session file while you're in there. So the capture-the-new-session-id must happen **after you detach** from that tmux session (when taco resumes), by diffing the sessions dir against the pre-launch snapshot.\n\nThere's an ambiguity worth flagging: if kiro spawns **subagents**, one chat can create *multiple* session files (I can see `\"session_created_reason\": \"subagent\"` in that very file). So a naive \"one new file = the session\" diff could pick the wrong one. The most reliable identifier is the **main** session — the one whose `cwd` matches the directory you launched in and whose `session_created_reason` is *not* `subagent`. I'll use that heuristic to pick the right new session.\n\nLet me lay out the concrete plan:\n\n**Provider interface + kiro impl** (`provider` package):\n```go\ntype Provider interface {\n    Name() string\n    StartCommand(dir, agent string) *exec.Cmd   // tmux new-session in dir running kiro-cli --agent\n    ResumeCommand(sessionID string) *exec.Cmd    // tmux + kiro-cli chat --resume-id <id>\n    SessionsDir() string\n    Agents() ([]string, error)                   // list *.json stems, skipping noise\n    DetectNewSession(before map[string]bool, dir string) (id string, ok bool)  // diff snapshot\n}\n```\n`kiroProvider` implements these with the exact commands you gave. Session start/resume run **inside tmux** (so they get a real terminal and persist), consistent with how repos launch.\n\n**`chats` package** (mirrors `repos`): persists `~/.taco/chats` as `chatName#sessionID` (I'll store the **session id**, not the full path, since the path is derivable as `<sessionsDir>/<id>.json` and the id is what `--resume-id` needs). Operations: load, add, delete, rename.\n\nWait — you specified `chatName#/path/to/kiro/chat/file`. Storing the **path** vs the **id**: `--resume-id` needs the id, and the id is the filename stem, so path and id are equivalent. I'll follow your spec and store the path, deriving the id from the filename stem when resuming. That keeps your file format as stated.\n\n**Chats tab UI**: list chat entries (reuse list/search/scroll). **Space** → agent picker (list from `Agents()`) → directory browser (reuse the add-wizard browser) → launch via `tea.ExecProcess`. On return, diff sessions dir, find the new session, write `chatName#path`. **Enter** on an existing chat → resume.\n\nTwo decisions I need from you before building:\n\n1. **Chat naming**: you said Space opens a directory browser to pick where to start. But the entry needs a `chatName`. Where does the name come from — do you want to **type a name** in the new-chat flow (I'd add a name field), or auto-derive it (e.g. from the directory + timestamp)?\n\n2. **Agent selection order**: you want to choose an agent when creating. So the new-chat flow is: **pick agent → pick directory → (name?) → launch**. Is that order right, and should agent selection be required or optional (kiro-cli default agent if skipped)?\n\nAnswer those and I'll build it in stages (provider interface + kiro impl first, then the chats store, then the Chats-tab UI), verifying each."
          }
        ]
      }

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "Good catch — you're right, there's a `\"title\"` field in the session JSON (it was `null` in that particular one because it was a fresh subagent session, but kiro does populate it on real chats). That changes chat naming for the better: instead of asking you to type a name, taco can **read the title from the session file** and use that as the chat name. Less friction, exactly your \"as little manual hassle as possible\" principle.\n\nSo the flow becomes: **pick agent → pick directory → launch**. No name prompt. On return, taco finds the new session file, reads its `title`, and stores the entry. Clean.\n\nBut `title` being `null` at creation time is the wrinkle I need to handle. When you *first* start a chat and immediately detach, kiro may not have set a title yet (it's often derived from your first message). So at capture time the title could still be `null`. I'll handle it gracefully:\n- If `title` is set → use it as the chat name.\n- If `title` is null/empty → fall back to something readable (e.g. the directory name + short id, or just \"untitled\"), and — better — **re-read the title from the file each time the Chats list renders**, so once kiro sets it, taco picks it up automatically without you doing anything.\n\nThat last point is actually the cleaner model: rather than freezing the name at capture time, taco stores the **session id/path** as the entry's identity and derives the **display name from the live title** in the file. So the list always reflects kiro's current titles, and renamed/late-titled sessions just show correctly. This also means taco's `chats` file could store just the path (as you specified: `chatName#path`) — but the `chatName` there becomes a cached/fallback, with the live title preferred.\n\nLet me confirm the title-handling approach before I build, since it shapes the chats store:\n\n**Option A (store name, static):** capture the title at creation, write `chatName#path`, never update it. Simple, but if the title was null at capture or changes later, the list is stale.\n\n**Option B (store path, derive name live):** the entry's identity is the path/session-id; the display name is read live from the file's `title` each render (falling back to the stored name or a placeholder if null). Always accurate, self-updating. Slightly more work (a small JSON read per listed chat, cheap and cacheable).\n\nI lean toward **B** — it matches how kiro actually works (titles appear/change over time) and needs no manual renaming. Your `chatName#path` format still works as the persisted fallback.\n\nWhich do you want — A (simple, static name) or B (live title from the file)? Once you pick, I'll start building the provider interface + kiro implementation."
          }
        ]
      }

                "command": "create",
                "content": "// Package provider defines the contract taco needs from a chat CLI (e.g.\n// kiro-cli) and concrete implementations of it.\n//\n// The design mirrors Java's interface + implementation: Provider is the\n// contract, and each concrete type (e.g. kiroProvider) satisfies it. Go uses\n// implicit (structural) satisfaction — no \"implements\" keyword — so a type is\n// a Provider simply by having the required methods.\npackage provider\n\nimport \"os/exec\"\n\n// Provider abstracts a chat CLI so taco can start, resume, and inspect chat\n// sessions without knowing provider-specific details.\ntype Provider interface {\n\t// Name is the human-readable provider name.\n\tName() string\n\n\t// StartCommand returns a command that starts a NEW chat in the given\n\t// working directory using the given agent (agent may be empty for the\n\t// provider default). The command is interactive and intended to be run\n\t// inside a tmux session.\n\tStartCommand(dir, agent string) *exec.Cmd\n\n\t// ResumeCommand returns a command that resumes the chat identified by\n\t// sessionID. Interactive; run inside tmux.\n\tResumeCommand(sessionID string) *exec.Cmd\n\n\t// SessionsDir is the directory where session files are stored.\n\tSessionsDir() string\n\n\t// Agents returns the available agent names.\n\tAgents() ([]string, error)\n\n\t// SessionSnapshot returns the set of currently existing session IDs. Used\n\t// before starting a chat so the newly created session can be detected\n\t// afterwards via DetectNewSession.\n\tSessionSnapshot() (map[string]bool, error)\n\n\t// DetectNewSession finds the session created since the given snapshot whose\n\t// working directory matches dir (preferring a top-level, non-subagent\n\t// session). Returns the new session ID and true, or \"\" and false.\n\tDetectNewSession(before map[string]bool, dir string) (string, bool)\n\n\t// SessionTitle returns the live display title for a session ID (may be\n\t// empty if the provider has not set one yet).\n\tSessionTitle(sessionID string) string\n\n\t// SessionCWD returns the working directory recorded for a session ID.\n\tSessionCWD(sessionID string) string\n}\n",
                "path": "/Users/egriham/repos/misc/taco/provider/provider.go"
              }
            }

          {
            "kind": "text",
            "data": "Now I understand the tmux pattern. For chats, the `StartCommand`/`ResumeCommand` need to run kiro *inside* a tmux session (in the chosen directory) so it persists and can be reattached, and after reattach kiro resumes. I'll build the kiro implementation to produce a `tmux new-session` that runs `kiro-cli` with the right args.\n\nThere's a design point: you said the *resume command is used after we reattach to that tmux session*. So the tmux session persists after you detach, and resuming means re-attaching to that tmux session (kiro is still running in it). But you also gave `kiro-cli chat --resume-id <id>` as the resume command. Let me reconcile: the tmux session may have ended (kiro exited) — in which case resume = new tmux session running `kiro-cli chat --resume-id <id>`. I'll model resume as starting a tmux session that runs the resume command. Let me build the kiro impl:"
